newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - India railways gather steam after 50 years.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - India railways gather steam after 50 years.

text.p: When India's rail minister paid a surprise visit to New Delhi station recently, he found filthy, rubbish-strewn platforms, people queuing at an unmanned ticket counter and no public information about the latest train crash.
He suspended three employees and sacked a senior station manager on the spot.
Such is the modern face of management at Indian Railways, which not so long ago shunned outside consultants because it had done well enough for decades without those "smart alecs".

True, the antique, sooty days of steam engines have been shunted into the sidings. And a staggering 12,500 trains run every day on some 63,000 km (39,375 miles) across this continent-sized country of 936 million people.

But ever since India inherited the century-old railways network when it won independence from Britain on August 15, 1947, its trains have scored high on charm and low on comfort, speed and efficiency.
OVERCROWDING, DELAYS, FILTHINESS...
In "No Full Stops in India", Mark Tully, who was the BBC's Delhi correspondent for several years, writes about a guide book to the railways' exam for recruitment to clerical grade.
The examinee, asked to write a 250-word essay describing a railway journey, was given a model answer.

"Railway journeys these days are fraught with disasters," it began. "Accidents and robberies are all too commonly associated with railway journeys and not without justification, too. Overcrowding, delays, filthiness and other general inconveniences have of course come to be regarded as normal features of a railway journey."
The 50 years have not passed, however, in complacency.
In 1990, the Railways Minister of the day, George Fernandes, made a plea for improvements to the overstretched suburban rail system of Bombay, a city of 13.5 million people.
"The Indian Railways have very strict rules on how many live animals -- cows, buffaloes, goats, donkeys etc. -- can be carried in a wagon of specified dimensions," he said.
"But no such rules and legislation govern the transportation of human beings -- old and young, men and women, boys and girls or even infants. Forty-three years after freedom!"
His words, unfortunately for some six million commuters who still cram like sardines into scruffy carriages or hang precariously from open doors, failed to have the desired effect.
BRAKES ON IMPROVEMENT
Efforts to smarten up stations, with their rag-tag armies of beggars, hawkers and ticket touts, have also hit the buffers.

A daily newspaper recently carried a photograph of people walking across some tracks after alighting from a rush-hour train. "They shy away from the foot overbridge as it has been turned into an open toilet," the caption explained.

The general manager of the Bombay-based Western Railway, N. Krithivasan, says there is much that the state-owned corporation can be proud of since independence, most notably "moving a vast humanity of passengers" and huge volumes of freight.
But he is unequivocal about the one key failing.
"Somehow, we fail to get adequate financial support for the ever-increasing demand for trains," Krithivasan says.
The Railways Ministry says that 10 percent of the ageing tracks need to be replaced and 20,000 wagons, 2,000 coaches and many engines are crying out for renewal every year.

The railway's net revenue in the 1996/97 financial year was just over $1 billion, so after forking out wages for 1.55 million people -- the biggest payroll in the world -- precious little is left for capital expenditure and investment.

This year, the government froze spending on maintenance and development at $2.32 billion. Needing more, the Indian Finance Railway Corporation has turned to the private sector, including the international bond market.
PRIVATISATION NOT ON THE AGENDA
But the growing sophistication of railway business managers would not appear to be matched by new attitudes in government.

In the name of providing a social service, privatisation is not on the agenda and loss-making lines to far-flung destinations will stay open. Fares -- the impecunious can travel the 1,400 km (875 miles) from Bombay to Delhi for as little as $5.60 -- will remain at rock-bottom prices.

Giri Patwardhan, a rail enthusiast since he was a boy some 70 years ago and a mine of train trivia, says provincial politics play a damaging role in the development of the railways, leading to new lines being built in the wrong places.
"If you want to have a viable rail network it has to stand on its own two feet," he says, arguing for more autonomy.
Still, the railways are trying to move with the times.

Western, one of the more progressive branches of Indian Railways, has computerised its passenger reservation system at many stations. It has even introduced the INMARSAT satellite telephone system on two of its express trains.
And, specially for the jubilee celebrations, Western will play patriotic songs and quotations from freedom fighters over its public address system.
